reason: Attacked and it holds. WORDING: the article was pulled as raw HTML and stripped rather than summarised, so the sentence was read as the page prints it. In the body of Secunda Secundae, question 58, article 1, the English Dominican Province text runs “Accordingly, this is a complete definition of justice; save that the act is mentioned instead of the habit... And if anyone would reduce it to the proper form of a definition, he might say that ‘justice is a habit whereby a man renders to each one his due by a constant and perpetual will’: and this is about the same definition as that given by the Philosopher (Ethic. v, 5) who says that ‘justice is a habit whereby a man is said to be capable of doing just actions in accordance with his choice.’” The shipped line is that clause exactly, in order, with the initial letter raised and the translation’s colon replaced by a full stop at the cut, which is the note’s own disclosure. Nothing is minted. LOCATOR: correct, and the stronger half of it was checked. The sentence stands in the respondeo, which this translation heads “I answer that”, and not in any Reply to Objection: in the retrieved text the three Replies follow it, the first beginning “Reply to Objection 1. Will here denotes the act, not the power”. Question 58, article 1, of the Secunda Secundae is right. TRANSLATION CREDIT: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province, second and revised edition, 1920, is the text that carries this wording. ATTRIBUTION: Aquinas, and the note is accurate about how he offers it. The definition’s ancestry is the Roman jurists, Ulpian in Justinian’s Digest, and the note says so rather than letting Aquinas appear to coin it; he then endorses it by equating it with Aristotle’s in the next clause, which the page shows. No misattribution-list trap applies. ONE CAUTION FOR THE EDITOR, NOT A REFUTATION: in the translation the sentence sits inside quotation marks and is introduced conditionally, “if anyone would reduce it to the proper form of a definition, he might say that”, so a reader with the page will find it as a reformulation rather than as a flat assertion. The note already states this, which is what the standard requires. SCOPE: the Summa is theology and philosophy, not scripture and not liturgy, so it is not the Library’s ground; no film, lyric, proverb, business writing or oratory; thirteenth century, so pre-1999.
